extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political science and public policy; leaders and communicators interested in public opinion and democratic processes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative and descriptive criteria about how public opinion is formed, how leaders manage and manipulate consent, and what constraints mass decision-making imposes on democracy. Useful for evaluating leadership, propaganda, and democratic procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader cultivation of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must cultivate symbols (flags, totems, words, doctrines) which concentrate disparate loyalties and conserve unity, providing a 'handle' to move a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols discharge emotion at a common target and blot out idiosyncratic ideas; effective leaders—even unbelieving ones—cherish symbols because they merge differences and enable collective action. Examples range from national flags to simplified ideological catch-phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols as double-edged instrument (solidarity vs. exploitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: While symbols create solidarity and enable coordinated action, they also enable exploitation by a few who choose concrete objectives, deflect criticism, and seduce followers into sacrifices they do not fully understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The symbol's power to siphon emotion from distinct ideas makes it both necessary in crises and potentially pernicious in peacetime; leaders may use symbols to hide failures or exaggerate successes, which can ultimately disintegrate the symbol and provoke upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of simplicity in mass decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any decision requiring mass participation must be presented in necessarily simple terms (typically yes/no), because the mass cannot handle complex, multifaceted choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms like initiatives, referenda, or even preferential ballots cannot obviate the need to create clear, simple issues; ballot measures are usually abbreviated and force binary responses, so the quality of the choices presented is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small leadership groups present choices to the many
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively small number of leaders or organizers formulate and present concrete choices which the larger public then registers—e.g., caucuses, nominating conventions, steering committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everyone who wishes to accomplish large-coalition objectives follows the example of professional politicians: the Many often elect only after the Few have nominated. The central fact remains that a small number of heads present a choice to a large group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masses need cues and suggestion to form opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most impressions from the 'invisible world' are formed as a kind of reverie and carry an aura of suggestion; people rarely consciously decide about distant events and look for cues (news framing, editorials, trusted advisers) indicating how to feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If news does not provide a suggested stance, people turn to editorials or advisers; until facts are formulated to allow a Yes/No feeling, the public remains unsettled. Thus framing and suggested reactions are central to opinion formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must consider morale when planning policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should evaluate decisions not only on merits but on their effects on the morale and capacities of those whose support they require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include wartime casualty reporting and withholding information to avoid breaking military morale; leaders calculate how much strain followers can bear before support dissolves, and plan actions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over information: officials act as censors/propagandists
rubrics_metrics.description: Every official, by deciding what facts to reveal and how to present them, functions in some degree as a censor and a propagandist, shaping public knowledge strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because leaders have better access to facts and to channels of publication, they can choose facts, settings, and guises that serve institutional safety or political ends; suppression or glossing of failures can create powerful public illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and unity can be necessary in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergency or eruptive situations, securing unity and flexibility without full public consent may be necessary; public debate or full disclosure can be more destructive than partial mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: commanders who kept dissent within small circles to preserve command cohesion (e.g., Foch during World War I). The need for secrecy must be weighed against democratic norms—leaders may legitimately avoid public 'rows on Olympus' to prevent dissolution of collective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture of consent is a refined, analytic art
rubrics_metrics.description: The creation of public consent has become a self-conscious, technically advanced practice grounded in psychological research and modern communications; persuasion now modifies political premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not merely sinister propaganda; it is often a routine organ of modern governance. Because persuasion is now analytic and systematic, knowledge of these methods will change political calculations and the assumptions of democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation and apparent consent may be illusory
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders may seek to bring subordinates into confidence to produce a feeling of freely willed consent, but when facts are complex this consultation often produces only an illusion of understanding and assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large percentages of people agree without the background or time to appreciate contingencies; hearing one's case in court and then seeing acceptable outcomes leads most to accept policies without scrutinizing how much their opinions mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programs must be rhetorically connected to existing feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: New policies succeed only when they are verbally and emotionally linked to feelings already vocalized in the mass; leaders vocalize prevalent opinions then translate them into actionable programs by analogy and association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial phase: leader identifies with familiar attitudes (stories, patriotism, grievances) to gain trust, then sets forth a plan that is connected enough to the mass's feelings to be accepted even if not fully understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence of policy affects leaders' freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders have greater freedom when the burdens or results of policies are remote, unseen, indirect, or deferred; conversely, visible, immediate costs constrain leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments prefer policies where costs fall on distant actors or are diffuse; visible phenomena (taxation, local shortages) produce pressure for immediate action. Political incentives favor solutions that minimize visible cost to voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political work often emphasizes visible small favors over broad policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians frequently focus on doing many small, visible services for constituents rather than attempting large, complex constructive policies that deal with remote causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes offering scapegoats, placating factions, rearranging jobs, or attending influential individuals; serving many people on small matters can be more electorally secure than tackling systemic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic ideal of spontaneously informed public is unrealistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical democratic assumption that reasoned political knowledge springs spontaneously from the mass is false; realistic opinion requires time, measurement, analysis, and self-criticism and will not prosper without institutional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because casual opinion arises from partial contact, tradition, and personal interest, developing informed political judgment needs deliberate effort and resources; without ingrained habits of analysis, democratic publics remain susceptible to 'buncombe' and manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mass is not an organism: collective thought differs from individual thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is a function of an organism; a mass lacks the integrated organismal capacity for synchronous invention of programs across many minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if exposed to identical stimuli, a mass would produce a distribution of responses that would only cohere as individuals verbalize and harden classifications; leaders who understand these emergent patterns can anticipate and shape outcomes.
